message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2024) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs that affect health or safety must be made promptly. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) of needed repairs.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may:
 • Withhold rent (after giving notice),
 • Make the repair yourself and deduct the cost from rent (after giving notice),
 • File a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable (usually not more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Keep receipts or proof of payment.
• If you’re late, communicate with the landlord and negotiate a payment plan if needed. | | **Entry & Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable” means a time that is convenient for both parties. | • Ask for a written notice of entry.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can refuse entry and document the incident. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income. | • Report discrimination to the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Lease Termination** | • For month‑to‑month leases, either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, you can break the lease only if the landlord breaches the lease or if you have a “just cause” (e.g., domestic violence, health hazard). | • Provide written notice and keep copies.
• If breaking the lease, negotiate a release or pay a penalty as specified in the lease. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas **eviction procedure**: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice to pay rent or quit, 30‑day notice to vacate for non‑payment, 60‑day notice for lease termination).
• After the notice period, the landlord files a **Petition for Eviction** in court. | • Respond to the eviction notice in writing.
• Attend the court hearing; you can present evidence of payment or lease violations. | | **Repair and Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from rent, but you must:
 • Give written notice of the defect and your intent to repair.
 • Keep receipts and provide them to the landlord. | • Document the defect and your repair work.
• If the landlord disputes the deduction, you can file a small claims case. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live in the property without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • If the landlord interferes (e.g., frequent unannounced visits, harassment), document incidents and notify the landlord in writing. | | **Insurance** | • While not required by law, it’s wise to have renter’s insurance covering personal property and liability. | • Obtain a policy that covers theft, fire, water damage, and liability. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas offers free or low‑cost legal aid for tenants (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center, local bar association referral services). | • Contact a local tenant advocacy group or legal aid office if you need help. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Understand all terms, including rent amount, due date, late fees, and notice periods. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and inspection reports. 3. **Know the Notice Requirements** – Landlords need 24‑hour notice for entry; you need 30‑day notice to terminate a month‑to‑month lease. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Write a formal notice for repairs; follow up if the landlord doesn’t respond. 5. **Keep Records of Payments** – Use bank transfers or checks that provide a receipt; avoid cash if possible. 6. **Seek Help Early** – If you face eviction or discrimination, contact a tenant rights organization or legal aid before the situation escalates. --- #### Useful Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Information on landlord‑tenant laws, complaint filing, and housing assistance. | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Handles discrimination complaints. | https://www.tchr.texas.gov | | **Texas Legal Services Center** | Free legal assistance for low‑income residents. | https://www.texaslegalservices.org | | **Local Bar Association** | Lawyer referral services. | Search online for your county bar association. | | **HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development)** | National fair housing resources. | https://www.hud.gov | --- ### Bottom Line As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, fair notice for entry, and protection against discrimination. If your landlord violates these rights, you can take steps ranging from written notices to legal action. Knowing the basics of the Texas landlord‑tenant law will empower you to protect your interests and resolve disputes more effectively.
